data.text:
As a young lawmaker, Renee must never forget that our nation’s memory is long and unforgiving. History teaches us that those who play with unrest often end up consumed by it. Mendiola is scarred with the blood of 1970 and 1987 and these are moments when disorder drowned out reason and left families mourning instead of marching forward. 

The Constitution is clear: any act that incites rebellion or disrupts public order is not a show of courage but a violation of the very mandate a legislator swore to uphold. At a time when the country fights to steady itself, adding fuel to the fire is not bravery but it is reckless ambition.

And let us name the shadow behind this unrest. The Dutertes and their circle, threatened by accountability and desperate to reclaim power without the people’s mandate, is moving pieces across institutions. From Senate manoeuvres to coordinated street agitation, to weaken the sitting President and destabilise the constitutional order. This is how power-grabs historically begin: small provocations that grow into manufactured chaos. A young legislator like you should be wise enough not to become another pawn in their game. 

Stand with law, with memory, with nation. Because in this fragile moment, the Philippines cannot afford leaders who mistake disorder for destiny.

Protests come amid widespread anger over billions of pesos spent on substandard or non-existent flood control infrastructure.
